Why Does a Wire Resist Electric Current?

Inside a metal wire, there are many free electrons. When the wire is connected to a battery, these electrons move. However, they cannot travel smoothly. Along their path are stationary metal atoms. Electrons frequently collide with these atoms, lose some of their motion, and are pushed forward again by the battery. These collisions are what we call electrical resistance.

Imagine a group of people walking through a hallway filled with pillars. The longer the hallway, the more pillars they must pass, making it harder to get through. The wider the hallway, the more paths are available at once, making it easier to pass. A hallway with tightly packed pillars is also harder to walk through than one with widely spaced pillars. This "pillar density" depends on the type of material, which scientists call resistivity. Different materials have different resistivities.

A student tests four copper wires. Wire Q is twice as long as wire P. Wire R has twice the cross-sectional area of wire P. Wire S is both twice as long and has twice the cross-sectional area of wire P. The resistances of P, Q, and R have already been measured, while S has not.

Based on the passage and diagram, choose the two correct statements! (Select 2 answers.)
opts: A longer wire has greater resistance because electrons must pass more obstructing atoms.
A thicker wire has greater resistance because electrons become crowded inside it.
The resistance of wire S is 2 Ω.
A copper wire and an iron wire of the exact same dimensions must have the same resistance.
Wire thickness does not affect resistance; only the wire's length matters.

html:
The Secret of Batteries Inside a Flashlight

Have you ever put batteries into a flashlight backward, only to find it wouldn't turn on? That happens because a battery has two terminals: a positive (+) terminal and a negative (−) terminal. In circuit diagrams, the + terminal is drawn as a long thin line, while the − terminal is drawn as a short thick line.

Each battery "pushes" electric current with a voltage of 1.5 V. When several batteries are connected in a row along a single path, their pushes combine according to the following rules:

  • Same direction (all long lines face the same side): their voltages are added together.
  • Opposite direction (long lines face different sides): the batteries oppose each other, so one battery subtracts from the voltage of the others.

This net voltage is what reaches the bulb. All bulbs in this problem are identical, and their brightness is determined as follows:

Net voltageBulb condition
3 VGlows brightly
1.5 VGlows dimly
0 VOff (no light)

One more thing: a bulb can only light up if the path is closed from end to end. An open switch acts just like a broken wire.

Based on the passage and diagram, determine whether each of the following statements is True or False!
opts: The bulb in Setup 2 glows more brightly than the bulb in Setup 1.
The bulb in Setup 1 glows brightly because it uses three batteries.
The bulbs in Setup 3 and Setup 4 are both off.

html:
The Gatekeeper Inside a Power Strip

A power strip contains a small safety component called a fuse. Think of a fuse as a building security guard: it monitors how much electric current enters all at once. If the passing current exceeds its limit, the fuse blows (melts) and stops all appliances so the wires do not overheat.

Every appliance plugged into the power strip has its own separate path, but all of their currents must pass through the fuse first. Therefore, the current flowing through the fuse is the sum of the currents of all appliances that are currently turned on. Appliances that are turned off are not counted.

A household power strip has a fuse rated at 10 A. Exactly 10 A is still safe, whereas anything above 10 A will blow the fuse. The current drawn by each appliance when turned on is shown below:

ApplianceCurrent when ON
Water heater5 A
Clothes iron3 A
Television2 A
Electric fan1 A

Based on the passage, choose the two correct statements! (Select 2 answers.)
opts: The water heater and the clothes iron can be turned on at the same time without blowing the fuse.
All four appliances can be turned on at the same time without blowing the fuse.
The current passing through the fuse is equal to the current of the single largest appliance.
Turning on the water heater, clothes iron, and electric fan together is safe, but also turning on the television will blow the fuse.
Low-current appliances like the electric fan are ignored by the fuse.

Why Do Bulbs Glow Brightly or Dimly?

A light bulb glows more brightly when the voltage across it is greater. Two identical bulbs that receive the same voltage will have the exact same brightness.

There are two ways to connect bulbs:

  • In a single row (series). The battery voltage is shared equally among identical bulbs. Because there is only one path, removing one bulb breaks the path and turns off all the bulbs.
  • In branching paths (parallel). Each bulb has its own separate path and receives the full voltage of the battery. Removing one bulb does not break the path to the other bulbs.

Electric Current is Like Water in Pipes

Imagine water flowing through a branching pipe. A junction point does not store water and does not create new water. Therefore, the amount of water flowing into a junction must equal the amount of water flowing out of it.

Electric current in wires behaves the exact same way. At every junction point, the total current entering equals the total current leaving. The unit of electric current is the ampere (A). The red arrows in the diagram show the direction of the current.

The diagram below shows a network of branching wires. A current of 10 A enters at junction P. At junction Q, the current along the lower path splits again. All paths eventually meet at junction R.

Based on the passage and diagram, choose the two correct statements! (Select 2 answers.)
opts: The current along path b is 6 A.

The current leaving junction R is less than 10 A because part of the current is used up along the paths.
The current along path c is greater than the current along path d.
The current leaving junction R is 10 A.

Testing Three Resistors

A resistor is a component that opposes electric current. The greater its resistance, the less current can pass through it at the same voltage. Resistance is calculated using the rule:

Resistance (Ω) = Voltage (V) ÷ Current (A)

A student measures the current through three resistors—P, Q, and S—while varying the voltage. The results are plotted on the graph below. Every point on a line represents a pair of voltage and current values for that resistor.

Rises and Drops in a Closed Loop

Imagine a roller coaster traveling around a closed track. After completing one full loop, the coaster returns to its starting height. Therefore, the total uphill climbs along the track must equal the total downhill drops.

In a closed electric circuit, a battery acts as an uphill climb (supplying voltage), while other components (resistors) act as downhill drops (using voltage). Around one complete closed loop, the net battery voltage equals the sum of the voltages across all receiving components.

When two batteries are connected in opposite directions, their voltages oppose each other, and the net voltage is the difference between them. In the diagrams below, the boxes represent receiving components along with their voltages.

The voltage across M₂ is 4 V.

html:
One Light Bulb, Two Switches

On a staircase in a multi-story house, a single light can often be turned on or off from either the upstairs or downstairs switch. This is done using two two-way switches, S₁ and S₂. The lever of each switch can touch only one of its two contacts at a time: the upper contact or the lower contact.

Two wires connect the two switches. The upper wire connects the upper contact of S₁ to the upper contact of S₂. The lower wire connects the lower contact of S₁ to the lower contact of S₂. Current from the battery enters the lever of S₁, passes through whichever contact it touches, and travels along the corresponding wire.

The bulb lights up only when a closed path is formed from the battery to the bulb and back to the battery. This means the current reaching the end of a wire must be able to enter the lever of S₂, which happens only if S₂ touches the contact at the end of that same wire.

Based on the passage and diagram, determine whether each of the following statements is True or False!
opts: The bulb lights up if S₁ touches the upper contact and S₂ also touches the upper contact.
The bulb lights up if S₁ touches the upper contact and S₂ touches the lower contact.
The bulb is currently lit. If both S₁ and S₂ are flipped to their opposite contacts at the same time, the bulb will turn off.

A Fan That Turns Itself On

Inside a computer, a cooling fan spins only when the temperature gets high. The secret is a temperature sensor connected in series with the fan and a 12 V battery. This sensor is a special resistor whose resistance decreases as the temperature rises.

In a series circuit, the battery voltage is shared among all components. The sum of the voltages across the sensor and the fan always equals the battery voltage (12 V). The component with greater resistance receives a larger share of the voltage.

The fan spins only when the voltage across it is 6 V or higher. Measurements at three different temperatures are shown in the table below:

Temperature Sensor resistance Voltage across fan
25 °CHigh2 V
40 °CMedium5 V
60 °CLow10 V

Based on the passage and table, determine whether each of the following statements is True or False!
opts: At 25 °C, the voltage across the temperature sensor is 10 V.
At 40 °C, the cooling fan is already spinning.
The higher the temperature, the greater the voltage received by the fan.

Narrower Road or Wider Road?

Imagine electric current as vehicles traveling on a road. Resistors act like road obstacles such as toll booths or narrow lanes. The total resistance of a circuit can be calculated from the battery voltage and total current:

Total Resistance (Ω) = Battery Voltage (V) ÷ Total Current (A)

A student uses one 12 V battery and three arrangements of identical resistors. Arrangement A uses a single resistor. Arrangement B adds a second identical resistor along the same path (in series). Arrangement C adds a second identical resistor on an extra parallel path (in parallel).

Arrangement Total current
A2 A
B1 A
C4 A

Based on the passage, diagram, and table, determine whether each of the following statements is True or False!
opts: The total resistance of Arrangement C is smaller than the total resistance of Arrangement A.
The total resistance of Arrangement B is 12 Ω.
Adding a resistor on an extra parallel path causes the total current from the battery to decrease.
